title: Italian Trade Agency to deepen Korea ties with food, beauty, and B2B push - Chosunbiz
text:
Italian Trade Agency to deepen Korea ties with food, beauty, and B2B push - CHOSUNBIZ 
 2026년 11월 16일(월) Industry Finance Real Estate IT Retail Science Policy Society International Entertainment Culture Sports English Retail Italian Trade Agency to deepen Korea ties with food, beauty, and B2B push 
 New Seoul chief Raimondo Lucariello says ITA will spotlight Italian organic foods and niche fragrances in Korea while scaling B2B meetings and e-commerce initiatives 
 입력 2026.11.16. 06:01 조선비즈 구글 검색 먼저 보기 "We will further increase opportunities for direct exchanges between Italian food producers and Korean distributors and buyers. We will keep holding B2B (business-to-business) meetings and plan to develop e-commerce (online retail) initiatives as well."
 Raimondo Lucariello, the new head of the Italian Trade Agency (ITA) office in Seoul, stated accordingly in an interview with ChosunBiz on the 5th. The ITA is a government agency that supports Italian companies' overseas expansion and export growth, similar to the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA) in Korea. Founded in 1926, it marks its 100th anniversary this year.
 The ITA has worked with major Korean retailers to help Italian consumer goods enter the Korean market. In September last year, it partnered with Coupang to launch an "Italian Market," showcasing more than 50 Italian brands of olive oil, coffee, cosmetics, and more. In August–September this year, it ran the "Viva Italia" campaign with CJ OnStyle, introducing Italian food, beauty, and home brands through a pop-up store, live commerce, and TV home shopping.
 Lucariello, 46, studied international relations in Naples, Italy, and pursued international economics and foreign trade at the ITA and European Union (EU) project management at LUISS University in Rome. After nearly 10 years at the Italian Banking Association, he joined the ITA in 2018, focusing on fashion, e-commerce, and retail. From 2022, he led the food and wine institutional sector at the New York office, and this month he took up his post in Seoul.
 Raimondo Lucariello, the new head of the Seoul office of the Italian Trade Agency (ITA), speaks at the ITA 100th anniversary event at High Street Italia in Gangnam District, Seoul, on the 5th. /Courtesy of Jeong Jae-hwon Lucariello sees Korea as a market with strong growth potential for Italian foods. Unlike the United States, where Italian food culture has long taken root, Korea is an open market where consumers value quality, innovation, and authenticity, and are receptive to premium imports and new culinary experiences, he said.
 He pointed to health-related foods as a particularly promising area. "Korean consumers are showing growing interest in organic products and superfoods," Lucariello said. "We see significant potential for Italian organic foods, natural juices, and nutrient-dense grains such as farro."
 He also flagged room to expand cooperation in beauty. Italy can raise awareness in Korea of its strengths in niche fragrances and professional skincare, aesthetics, and hair care, and broaden collaboration beyond finished goods exports to technology exchanges and joint ventures. The following is an interview in Q&A format.
 —What does the Korean market mean for Italian companies? 
 "Korea is a promising market for Italian companies because consumers are increasingly interested in high-quality food, wine, and lifestyle products. In wine especially, more consumers are learning about and enjoying Italy's native grape varieties and diverse wines. In food as well, Italian cuisine is already widely loved in Korea, but there is ample room to expand the presence of a wider range of Italian foods in everyday consumption."
 —You handled food and wine in the United States. How does Korea differ? 
 "The U.S. is a mature market where Italian food culture is long established. Korean consumers value quality, innovation, and authenticity, and they are open to new culinary experiences. Rather than simply increasing exports, the goal is to build sustainable demand for a diverse range of Italian products."
 —Which Italian foods have strong growth potential in Korea? 
 "Interest in healthy lifestyles, organic products, and so-called 'superfoods' is rising. We see strong growth potential for Italian organic foods, natural juices, and grains like farro. It is important to communicate these products' nutritional qualities, origins, and the many ways to use them."
 —Is there an aspect of Italian food culture you want to newly introduce to Korean consumers? 
 "So far, promotion has focused more on individual products and items than on specific regions. Extra virgin olive oil produced in many regions is a prime example. Going forward, I expect more opportunities to highlight each region's traditions, specialties, and cultural heritage."
 Italian pasta, tomato sauce, olive oil, and wine products imported and distributed in Korea. /Courtesy of Jeong Jae-hwon —How will you expand cooperation with Korean retailers? 
 "We will increase opportunities for direct exchanges between Italian food producers and Korean distributors and buyers. We will continue B2B (business-to-business) meetings and e-commerce projects, and we plan to invite Korean industry officials to trade shows and business events in Italy. Our goal is to help companies in both countries build long-term distribution partnerships."
 —Italy is also known as a beauty powerhouse. How do you see collaboration with K-beauty? 
 "Italy's beauty industry is competitive thanks to high-quality ingredients, manufacturing technology, and a long manufacturing tradition. We are especially strong in niche fragrances and professional skincare, aesthetics, and hair care. These categories still have considerable room to grow awareness and the broader market base in Korea.
 Given the size and global influence of Korea's beauty industry, there is substantial potential for collaboration beyond finished goods sales through technology exchanges and joint ventures. Combining Italy's manufacturing expertise with the Korean market's innovation capabilities would open new business opportunities for both countries' beauty industries."
 —As the new head of the Seoul office, what will you prioritize? 
 "The ITA needs to strengthen its role as a strategic partner to companies beyond traditional export promotion. In addition to the established 'Made in Italy' areas, I want to expand cooperation in technology, advanced manufacturing, and industrial innovation.
 We also plan to encourage Korean investment in Italy. The goal is to promote long-term industrial cooperation and mutual investment beyond simple trade."
